MovieScript:
The visiting room of the federal penitentiary was a sterile box of cinderblocks and cold fluorescent light. It smelled of floor wax and old coffee.

Jimmy sat at the small, bolted-down table, his orange jumpsuit a loud, garish stain against the grey walls. He looked older—the bravado of Saul Goodman had been stripped away, leaving only the tired remains of the man underneath.

The door buzzed, a harsh, mechanical rasp. Kim Wexler stepped inside.

She looked like a ghost from a life he had burned to the ground. She didn't say anything at first. She didn't have to. She walked to the table with that same determined, rhythmic stride he had known for twenty years. She sat across from him, her eyes searching his face for a trace of the man she used to love.

Without a word, she reached into her bag and pulled out a pack of cigarettes. She tapped one out and handed it to him.

Jimmy took it, his fingers trembling just enough to notice. He leaned forward. Kim struck a match. The flame was a tiny, flickering sun in the center of the room. As she held it to his cigarette, the world seemed to fall away—the prison walls, the eighty-six-year sentence, the wreckage of their lives. For a fleeting second, the scene shifted into a memory of the dark hallway at Hamlin, Hamlin & McGill, where their shadows used to dance against the glass.

He took a long drag, the cherry of the cigarette glowing bright. He exhaled a cloud of grey lace.

"You had them middle-of-the-road," Kim said softly, her voice steady but fragile. "You had them down to seven years."

Jimmy looked at the smoke drifting toward the ceiling. He had sabotaged his own plea deal. He had confessed to everything, not for the law, but for her. To show her that he was finally willing to take the hit.

"But with good behavior," Jimmy said, a ghost of a smirk playing on his lips, "who knows?"

Kim didn't smile. She just watched him, her heart breaking in the silence. They shared the cigarette, passing it back and forth like a sacred relic. It was the only language they had left—a shared habit, a shared sin, a shared history.

When the guard finally came to take him back, Jimmy stood up. He didn't look back until he reached the gated fence of the yard. Through the chain-link and the barbed wire, he saw her standing by her car in the parking lot.

He raised his hands, his fingers shaped into the familiar "finger guns" he used to fire when life was a game they were winning together. Bang, bang.

Kim stood motionless. She didn't fire back. She only watched him through the wire, her hand resting on the cold metal of the fence, until the shadows of the prison finally swallowed him whole.
